source_text: Cunctarum origo virtutum in rationabili animo sita est, et affectus omnes per quos aut fructuose aut steriliter boni sumus, in subiecto sunt mentis nostrae, prudentia, iustitia, temperantia, fortitudo. Horum igitur affectuum vis cum sit in omnibus naturaliter non tamen ad unum finem in omnibus properat: sed pro iudicio voluntatis, cuius nutui serviunt, aut ad aeterna, aut ad temporalia diriguntur. Quod cum fit, non in eo quod sunt, non in eo quod agunt, sed in eo solo variant quod merentur. Nec nominis sui igitur possunt, nec generis sustinere dispendium, sed solius quod appetiverunt praemii aut amplitudine ditantur, aut exilitate frustrantur Virtus est animi habitus, naturae modo atque rationi consentaneus

pass_b_english: The origin of every virtue lies in the rational soul. All the dispositions through which we are good, either fruitfully or fruitlessly, have their foundation in our mind: prudence, justice, self-control, and courage. Although the power of these dispositions is naturally present in everyone, it does not hasten toward the same goal in everyone. Instead, according to the judgment of the will whose direction they obey, they are directed either toward eternal things or toward temporary things. When this happens, they differ neither in what they are nor in what they do, but only in what they deserve. They therefore cannot suffer any loss of their name or their kind; they are simply enriched by the greatness of the reward they sought, or disappointed by its smallness.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)
